---
title: "Plots with matplotlib and plotnine"
---

A basemap goes under your data: `m.add_to(ax)` in matplotlib,
`ggplot(df) + m` in plotnine. The plot gives what a basemap on its own needs
from you: the extent (the axes' limits), the CRS (the basemap is warped into
it, so it lines up with the data), the image size (the axes) and the dpi (on
screen 96 x the screen's pixel ratio, in `savefig(dpi=300)` 300, in PDF and
SVG 300). It renders when the figure is drawn, so panning, zooming and
saving draw it afresh, and it credits the provider in the corner.

```{python}
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore", message=".*centroid.*")

import basemapper as bm
import geodatasets
import geopandas as gpd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

nc = gpd.read_file(geodatasets.get_path("geoda.sids"))
```

## matplotlib

`m.add_to(ax)` draws under what the axes already show, and returns the
basemap's artist. Plain axes carry no CRS, so give it the data's with
`crs=` (cartopy GeoAxes are read). `bm.add_basemap(ax, style, ...)` is the
same in one call:

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc.assign(rate=nc.SID79 / nc.BIR79 * 1000).plot(
    ax=ax, column="rate", cmap="OrRd", alpha=0.8, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2,
    legend=True, legend_kwds={"label": "SIDS per 1,000 births, 1979", "shrink": 0.7},
)
bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Positron").add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### Projected data

The basemap is drawn in Web Mercator and warped into the axes' CRS, so it
lines up with data in any CRS. Here North Carolina's state plane
(EPSG:32119), with the counties' centroids sized by births:

```{python}
nc_sp = nc.to_crs(32119)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc_sp.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="0.15", linewidth=0.3)
nc_sp.centroid.plot(ax=ax, markersize=nc_sp.BIR74 / 300, color="#D96E34", alpha=0.7)
bm.add_basemap(ax, "Esri.WorldTopoMap", crs=nc_sp.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### A quieter basemap

For a data map, a basemap often reads better without its labels, faded, or
with only some of its features. Filters belong to the style (see [Stacking,
labels and features](04-layers.qmd)); `alpha` fades the layer:

```{python}
quiet = bm.style("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", features=["-labels", "-roads", "-rail"])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc.assign(share=nc.NWBIR74 / nc.BIR74).plot(
    ax=ax, column="share", cmap="viridis", edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.2, legend=True,
    legend_kwds={"label": "Share of births, non-white, 1974", "shrink": 0.7},
)
bm.basemap(quiet).add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs, alpha=0.6)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### More detail, or sharper

The plot fixes the extent and the image's pixels, so the zoom follows from
the dpi. A `zoom` of your own gives more (or less) detail: the dpi then
follows (an *effective dpi*, reported once as a `BasemapAdjustment`), and
the style's labels are drawn at that dpi.

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.5))
nc.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="0.2", linewidth=0.3)
ax.set_xlim(-80, -77.5)
ax.set_ylim(35, 36.5)
with warnings.catch_warnings():
    warnings.simplefilter("ignore", bm.BasemapAdjustment)
    bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", zoom=8).add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

The basemap follows the axes, so setting their limits zooms it in, with
detail to match:

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 5.2))
nc.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="yellow", linewidth=1)
for _, row in nc.iterrows():
    p = row.geometry.representative_point()
    if -76.9 < p.x < -75.4 and 35.0 < p.y < 36.0:
        ax.annotate(row.NAME, (p.x, p.y), color="white", fontsize=9, fontweight="bold", ha="center")
ax.set_xlim(-76.9, -75.4)
ax.set_ylim(35.0, 36.0)
bm.add_basemap(ax, "Esri.WorldImagery", crs=nc.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### Clipping

`clip` draws the basemap only inside a layer's polygons, or outside them
with `bm.outside()`. In a plot, the plot still gives the extent: the clip is
a mask. Here the state in colour over a faded copy:

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="white", linewidth=0.2)
bm.basemap("Esri.WorldImagery").add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs, alpha=0.35, attribution=False)
bm.basemap("Esri.WorldImagery", clip=nc).add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs)
ax.set_axis_off()
```

### Credits

The credit line is on by default. `attribution=False` turns it off;
`get_attribution()` returns the text, for a caption:

```{python}
gray = bm.basemap("Esri.WorldGrayCanvas")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 3.6))
nc.boundary.plot(ax=ax, color="steelblue", linewidth=0.4)
gray.add_to(ax, crs=nc.crs, attribution=False)
ax.set_axis_off()
fig.text(0.98, 0.02, bm.get_attribution(gray), ha="right", fontsize=6, color="0.4")
```

## plotnine

Add a basemap to a plotnine plot like a layer. plotnine has no spatial
coordinates: the basemap reads the CRS of a GeoDataFrame's data, else takes
`geom_basemap(crs=...)`, else longitude / latitude. `bm.geom_basemap()`
builds one from `basemap()`'s arguments:

```{python}
from plotnine import aes, geom_map, ggplot, scale_fill_distiller, theme, theme_void

(
    ggplot(nc)
    + bm.basemap("OpenFreeMap.Positron")
    + geom_map(aes(fill="BIR79"), alpha=0.75, color="white", size=0.2)
    + scale_fill_distiller(type="seq", palette="Blues", direction=1, name="Births, 1979")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.6))
)
```

Raster and vector basemaps, stacks and filters work the same way; here
shaded relief under a vector basemap's labels:

```{python}
from plotnine import geom_point, scale_size_area

relief = ["Esri.WorldShadedRelief", bm.style("OpenFreeMap.Liberty", features="labels")]
centroids = nc.assign(x=nc.centroid.x, y=nc.centroid.y)

(
    ggplot(centroids)
    + bm.basemap(relief)
    + geom_map(fill=None, color="#333333", size=0.25)
    + geom_point(aes("x", "y", size="BIR74"), color="#D96E34", alpha=0.7)
    + scale_size_area(max_size=6, name="Births, 1974")
    + theme_void()
    + theme(figure_size=(8, 3.6))
)
```

## Saving

`savefig()` draws the basemap again at the file's dpi: the same map, sharp
at that resolution. A PDF or SVG gets it at 300 dpi.

```{python}
#| eval: false
fig.savefig("nc.png", dpi=300)
fig.savefig("nc.pdf")
```
